description: DecZero is an Ecuadorian multidisciplinary team that brings together talent from the country's three mainland regions: Coast, Highlands, and Amazon. Our name stands for Declination 0° (Dec = 0°), the Celestial Equator, the privileged vantage point (0, 0, 0) from which both celestial hemispheres can be observed. Uniting backgrounds in physics, data analysis, UX/UI design, and science communication, we turn open NASA data into clear, interactive, and evidence-driven tools.
summary:
We developed HAWAPACHA (from the Kichwa hawa pacha, "celestial space"), a public web tool that lets anyone enter a sky position (RA and Dec) and explore a time sequence of real SPHEREx infrared images. The app queries NASA's IRSA archive, reads the pixels from the public cloud copy, aligns the exposures north-up on a common grid, and combines them by observing period, so an object that moves stands out against the fixed stars. It includes the five challenge targets, a difference image, markers for the position expected from catalogue proper motion, plain-language guidance, and a public findings board where reviewers check each report against catalogues.
HAWAPACHA addresses the challenge by removing the technical work of finding, downloading, and aligning SPHEREx cutouts, and by keeping every step visible: the user sees real pixels, not a classifier's verdict. We validated it on real data: the measured shifts of Barnard's Star and Epsilon Indi B match their catalogue proper motions to within about one arcsecond.
It matters because it opens NASA's SPHEREx archive to citizen scientists, built by a student team in Ecuador, on the equator, and offers a reproducible way to look for faint moving objects such as a possible Planet X.
details:
HAWAPACHA is a public web app: https://deczero-bggaafdwwenl9wrdvzjlwn.streamlit.app/

1. Point. The user types any sky position (RA and Dec, in degrees or sexagesimal) and chooses one of the six SPHEREx detectors, or opens one of the five challenge targets with one click.

2. Fetch. The app asks NASA's IRSA archive which SPHEREx Level 2 spectral images cover that position and reads small cutouts from the public IRSA copy on AWS Open Data.

3. Compare. Every cutout is reprojected onto a common grid with north up and east left. Two views are offered: one frame per observing period (the median of that period's images, best for motion) or one frame per exposure. The user moves a slider, plays an animation, downloads it as a GIF, or opens a difference image (last period minus first).

An amber ring marks the centre of the view and a turquoise cross-hair marks where the catalogue position and proper motion place each target on that date. Pixels without data are drawn in purple so they are not mistaken for dark sky. A help window uses real crops to show what "it moved" looks like and what can fool the eye.

Anyone can report what they notice. A report can carry the sky position of a spot marked on the frame, and is published on a public findings board where a reviewer checks it against catalogues and signs a verdict.

Validation

We measured the shift of the challenge targets between their first and last observing periods on real SPHEREx images. Epsilon Indi B moved +5.1″ east, −3.9″ north (expected +5.7″, −3.6″) and Barnard's Star −0.5″, +10.2″ (expected −0.8″, +10.3″). The two variable stars, used as controls, showed no motion. WISE 0855 appears as a faint candidate detection only in the stacked frames.

Benefits and intended impact

Finding, downloading, and aligning SPHEREx cutouts normally takes code and astronomy training. HAWAPACHA reduces that to typing coordinates, so students and citizen scientists can inspect any patch of the SPHEREx sky and take part in the search for faint moving objects such as a possible Planet X.

Tools

Python and Streamlit, with Astropy, astroquery, PyVO, reproject, photutils, NumPy, SciPy, Matplotlib and Pillow; three.js for the animated header; GitHub Issues as the public store of reports; Streamlit Community Cloud for hosting. Code: https://github.com/JMVP0016/DECZERO

Creativity

The name comes from the Kichwa hawa pacha, "celestial space", linking the project to our team's home in Ecuador, on the equator. The findings board turns a viewer into a small citizen-science workflow: observers report, reviewers verify, and every step has a public timestamp.

What we considered

- Honesty about limits. The app does not detect anything by itself, and brightness changes of the variable stars cannot be measured here: their cores saturate, and each exposure sees a different wavelength. The app says so on screen.

- Reliability. The five targets are stored in the repository, so the demo works even when the archive is slow.

- Accessibility. Plain-language help, a phone layout, and a white-sky option for contrast.

- Privacy. Viewing needs no account; reporting stores only a chosen nickname.
